items.name: ACE inhibitors
items.how: Block ACE → ↓ angiotensin II and aldosterone; ↑ bradykinin
hx: Block renin → ↓ angiotensin I and aldosterone; ↑ bradykinin
Renin actually rises on ACE inhibitors; they act a step later, on angiotensin-converting enzyme.
Block ACE → ↑ angiotensin II breakdown; ↓ bradykinin
Bradykinin rises, not falls: ACE normally breaks it down (hence the cough).
Block aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal → ↓ Na⁺ retention; ↑ K⁺ loss
Aldosterone falls only indirectly, and K⁺ is retained, not lost.
items.sewhy: ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so it builds up (cough, angioedema). Less angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole (creatinine rises) and lowers BP (first-dose hypotension), and less aldosterone means the kidney keeps potassium.

ci.why: Fetotoxic in 2nd–3rd trimester: fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, skull defects
x: Cross into breast milk and cause neonatal hypotension
That's about breastfeeding (enalapril is actually used then); the harm is to the fetal kidneys in pregnancy.
Raise uterine bradykinin → preterm contractions and labour
No: the harm is fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios and skull defects.
Raise maternal angiotensin II → pre-eclampsia in the 3rd trimester
They lower angiotensin II; the danger is fetotoxicity in the 2nd–3rd trimester.

ci.why: GFR depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole; blocking it collapses filtration → AKI
x: Angiotensin II dilates the afferent arteriole; removing it starves the glomerulus → ischaemic AKI
Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole; losing that is what collapses GFR.
Rising bradykinin constricts the narrowed renal arteries, cutting renal blood flow → AKI
Bradykinin dilates vessels; the problem is losing efferent constriction.
Renin from the ischaemic kidneys rises further and drives malignant hypertension
Renin does rise, but BP falls; the danger is filtration collapsing (AKI).

ci.why: Bradykinin build-up can swell the airway
x: Histamine release from mast cells can swell the airway
ACE-inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-driven, so antihistamines help little.
IgE antibodies to the drug cause anaphylactic swelling
It isn't allergic; bradykinin that ACE would normally break down builds up.
Angiotensin II build-up increases airway capillary leak
Angiotensin II falls on ACE inhibitors; bradykinin is what accumulates.

ci.why: Less aldosterone means less K⁺ is excreted
x: They shift K⁺ out of cells into the blood
No shift between cells and blood; less aldosterone means the kidney keeps K⁺.
More angiotensin II means more K⁺ is reabsorbed
Angiotensin II falls; it's the drop in aldosterone that retains K⁺.
They block K⁺ secretion directly in the loop of Henle
The effect is indirect, through less aldosterone in the collecting duct.

ci.why: "Triple whammy" for AKI: pause on sick days
x: Together they cause hyponatraemic seizures: stop permanently
The risk is AKI, and only during dehydrating illness: pause, then restart.
NSAIDs stop ACE inhibitors being absorbed, so BP control is lost
No absorption effect; together they cut glomerular filtration (AKI).
Dehydration plus bradykinin triggers angioedema: avoid for good
Angioedema isn't linked to dehydration; the issue is sick-day AKI.

items.name: ARBs

uses.t: Hypertension (ACEi intolerant, or Black patients with CCB)

items.how: Block angiotensin II AT1 receptors; no effect on bradykinin, so no cough
hx: Block angiotensin II AT2 receptors; raise bradykinin, but without cough
They block AT1 (the receptor behind vasoconstriction and aldosterone); bradykinin is unaffected.
Inhibit aldosterone synthase in the adrenal; no effect on bradykinin
Aldosterone falls only because AT1 receptors are blocked.
Block ACE in the kidney only, sparing lung bradykinin, so no cough
ARBs don't touch ACE at all; they block the AT1 receptor.
items.sewhy: Blocking angiotensin II receptors lowers BP, reduces aldosterone (potassium rises) and relaxes the efferent arteriole (creatinine rises); bradykinin is unaffected, so no cough.

x: Cause neonatal cough and wheeze after birth
The harm is fetal renal failure and oligohydramnios, as with ACE inhibitors.
Raise maternal potassium enough to cause fetal arrhythmias
No; they damage the fetal kidneys in the 2nd–3rd trimester.
Trigger maternal angioedema more often in pregnancy
Not the reason: like ACE inhibitors they are fetotoxic.

ci.why: Removes the angiotensin II support of GFR → AKI
x: Raises bradykinin, constricting the stenosed arteries → AKI
ARBs don't raise bradykinin; GFR falls because efferent tone is lost.
Causes renal artery thrombosis behind the stenosis
No clotting effect; removing efferent constriction drops GFR.
Blocks renin release, so the kidneys can't respond
Renin rises on ARBs; the problem is losing angiotensin II's support of GFR.

ci.why: Dual RAAS blockade ↑ AKI and hyperkalaemia without benefit
x: ARBs stop ACE inhibitors being absorbed, so neither works
No absorption interaction; dual blockade adds harm without benefit.
The combination doubles bradykinin → angioedema in most patients
ARBs don't raise bradykinin; the harms are AKI and hyperkalaemia.
Dual RAAS blockade ↑ hyponatraemia and gout without benefit
The real harms are AKI and hyperkalaemia.
Pushes K⁺ out of cells by blocking insulin release
No effect on insulin; less aldosterone means less K⁺ is excreted.
Blocks K⁺ channels in the thick ascending limb
The effect is through less aldosterone in the collecting duct.
Increases angiotensin II-driven K⁺ reabsorption
Angiotensin II's effects are blocked; aldosterone falls, so K⁺ is retained.

items.name: Sacubitril/valsartan
hx: Neprilysin activator (↓ natriuretic peptides) + ARB
It inhibits neprilysin, so natriuretic peptides rise.
Neprilysin inhibitor (↑ natriuretic peptides) + ACE inhibitor
Pairing with an ACE inhibitor causes angioedema; sacubitril is paired with valsartan, an ARB.
Natriuretic peptide receptor blocker + aldosterone antagonist
It boosts natriuretic peptides by stopping their breakdown, and contains an ARB.
items.sewhy: Valsartan blocks angiotensin II (hypotension, high potassium, renal effects), and sacubitril stops neprilysin breaking down bradykinin, so angioedema can occur.

x: Both block AT1 receptors → severe hypotension
ACE inhibitors don't block AT1; the danger is bradykinin build-up.
Both raise potassium → cardiac arrest
Hyperkalaemia is a caution, but the 36-hour gap is about angioedema.
ACE inhibitors displace sacubitril from plasma proteins
No protein-binding interaction; additive bradykinin causes angioedema.
Same histamine mechanism
Not histamine: neprilysin breaks down bradykinin, so it accumulates.
Valsartan is cross-allergic with the original trigger
Not an allergy; sacubitril stops bradykinin being broken down.
Raised angiotensin II swells the airway
Valsartan blocks angiotensin II's effects; bradykinin causes the swelling.
Contains an ACE inhibitor (teratogenic)
It contains valsartan, an ARB, which is fetotoxic.
Neprilysin is needed for placental growth
The reason is the fetotoxic ARB component.
Natriuretic peptides trigger preterm labour
Not the reason; it contains an ARB.
Raised ammonia → encephalopathy
No ammonia effect; the liver clears it, so exposure rises.
Causes cholestatic jaundice
Not the reason; poor liver metabolism raises drug exposure.
Blocks albumin synthesis → oedema
No; the liver can't clear it, so levels rise.

items.name: Beta-blockers
items.how: Block β1 (± β2) → ↓ heart rate, contractility and renin
hx: Block β1 (± β2) → ↑ heart rate and contractility; ↓ renin
Blocking β1 slows the heart and weakens contraction.
Open K⁺ channels in the SA node → ↓ heart rate and renin
They block β-adrenoceptors; there's no direct K⁺ channel action.
Block noradrenaline release from sympathetic nerves → ↓ heart rate
Noradrenaline is still released; its β receptors are blocked.
items.sewhy: Blocking β1 slows the heart and lowers output (bradycardia, fatigue, hypotension); blocking β2 constricts airways and peripheral vessels (bronchospasm, cold hands). They also blunt the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia and act centrally (nightmares).

ci.why: β2 blockade constricts airways; can cause fatal bronchospasm
x: β1 blockade constricts airways; can cause fatal bronchospasm
Airway smooth muscle relaxes through β2, so blocking β2 is the danger.
Lower cardiac output means less inhaled salbutamol reaches the lungs
Inhaled salbutamol acts locally; β2 blockade constricts the airways.
They thicken airway mucus, plugging the small airways
Not the mechanism; β2 blockade constricts airway smooth muscle.
Speeds AV conduction → VT
Beta-blockers slow AV conduction, worsening the block.
Lowers potassium, triggering ectopic beats
No K⁺-lowering effect; the issue is slower AV conduction.
Causes vasospasm in the nodal artery
Not the reason; they further slow the AV node.

ci.c: Acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic shock
ci.why: ↓ contractility worsens output; start only once stable
x: ↑ afterload worsens output; never use in heart failure
Beta-blockers are a mainstay of stable HFrEF; the issue is starting during decompensation.
Causes fluid retention, so avoid lifelong
Not lifelong: start once the patient is stable.
↑ heart rate raises O₂ demand; start only once stable
They slow the heart; the risk is weaker contraction while decompensated.
Combined K⁺ retention → hyperkalaemia
Neither raises K⁺ much; together they block the AV node.
Combined bronchospasm → respiratory arrest
Verapamil doesn't constrict airways; the danger is AV-node block.
Opposing effects on the AV node cancel out
They add together: profound bradycardia or asystole.

ci.why: Hides tremor and palpitations, the warning signs of a hypo
x: Hides sweating, the main warning sign of a hypo
Sweating is cholinergic and persists; it's tremor and palpitations that get masked.
Raises blood glucose, so insulin doses need doubling
Small glucose effects aside, the problem is masking hypo warning signs.
Blocks insulin release, tipping patients into DKA
Not DKA; they hide the adrenergic warning signs of a hypo.
Non-selective agents are preferred because they also dilate airways
Non-selective agents block β2 and can constrict airways; cardioselective ones are preferred.
They raise CO₂ retention, so oxygen targets must drop
No; cardioselective agents are usually tolerated, so don't withhold them.
All beta-blockers must be stopped once COPD is diagnosed
Wrong: cardioselective agents are usually tolerated (unlike in asthma).

items.name: Dihydropyridine CCBs
items.how: Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in arterioles → vasodilation
hx: Open K⁺ channels in arterioles → vasodilation
That's how nicorandil and minoxidil work; amlodipine blocks L-type Ca²⁺ channels.
Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in veins → ↓ preload
They mainly dilate arterioles, lowering afterload.
Raise intracellular Ca²⁺ in arterioles → vasodilation
Less Ca²⁺ entry relaxes smooth muscle; more Ca²⁺ would constrict it.
items.sewhy: They dilate arterioles strongly: flushing and headache, reflex tachycardia, and ankle oedema because arterial dilation raises capillary pressure (diuretics don't fix it). Gum overgrowth is a fibroblast effect.

ci.why: Vasodilation with a fixed outflow → hypotension and syncope
x: Speeds valve calcification → rapid progression
No effect on calcification; vasodilation against a fixed outflow drops BP.
Slows the heart, cutting cardiac output
Dihydropyridines barely slow the heart; the issue is vasodilation.
Raises afterload, straining the left ventricle
They lower afterload; with a fixed valve, BP falls (syncope).
Bradycardia lowers coronary perfusion
Nifedipine causes reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia.
Raises afterload on the ischaemic heart
It lowers afterload; the reflex tachycardia is the problem.
Promotes platelet aggregation in the coronaries
No platelet effect; reflex tachycardia raises O₂ demand.

items.name: Rate-limiting CCBs
items.how: Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in the heart → ↓ AV conduction, rate and contractility
hx: Block Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum → ↓ contractility only
They block L-type channels in the cell membrane, which also slows the SA and AV nodes.
Block Na⁺ channels in the heart → ↓ AV conduction, rate and contractility
Na⁺ channel block is class I action; these are Ca²⁺ channel blockers (class IV).
Open cardiac K⁺ channels → hyperpolarise nodal cells and slow the rate
They block Ca²⁺ entry; there's no K⁺ channel opening.
items.sewhy: Verapamil and diltiazem act on the heart: slowing the SA and AV nodes (bradycardia, heart block) and reducing contractility. Verapamil also relaxes gut smooth muscle, causing constipation.

x: Positive inotropy exhausts the failing heart
They weaken contraction (negative inotropy), which worsens HFrEF.
Vasodilation causes fluid retention that worsens failure
The main harm in HFrEF is negative inotropy.
Raised afterload worsens failure
They lower afterload; the problem is weaker contraction.
Lowers K⁺, destabilising the conducting system
No K⁺ effect; they directly slow the SA and AV nodes.
Causes spasm of the nodal artery
They relieve coronary spasm; the issue is depressed nodal conduction.
Increases contractility, provoking arrhythmias
They reduce contractility and depress nodal conduction.
Severe hypertension from opposing effects
Both lower BP and heart rate; together they can stop the heart.
Severe bronchospasm
Verapamil doesn't constrict airways; the danger is bradycardia or asystole.
Hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest
Not through potassium; both block the AV node.

items.name: Thiazide-like diuretics
items.how: Block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ co-transporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule
hx: Block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ co-transporter in the proximal convoluted tubule
NCC sits in the distal convoluted tubule.
Block epithelial Na⁺ channels (ENaC) in the collecting duct
ENaC is amiloride's target; thiazides block NCC in the distal tubule.
Block Cl⁻ secretion into the distal convoluted tubule
They stop Na⁺/Cl⁻ being reabsorbed, not Cl⁻ being secreted.
items.sewhy: Blocking distal sodium reabsorption loses sodium (hyponatraemia) and, by delivering more sodium to the collecting duct, potassium. They reduce urate excretion (gout), impair insulin release (hyperglycaemia) and increase calcium reabsorption.

x: Increases urate production in the liver → attacks
They don't raise production; they compete with urate for excretion.
Lowers urine pH so urate crystallises in joints
Serum urate rises because the kidney excretes less.
Raises calcium, forming crystals in joints
Calcium crystals cause pseudogout; thiazides trigger gout by retaining urate.
Corrects both too quickly
They cause Na⁺ and K⁺ loss, worsening both.
Masks both on blood tests
No masking; they lower Na⁺ and K⁺ further.
Raises sodium but lowers potassium
They lower both.
Increases gut calcium absorption
That's vitamin D's action; thiazides cut urinary calcium loss.
Releases calcium from bone
That's PTH's action; thiazides keep calcium by reducing urinary loss.
Increases PTH secretion
No direct PTH effect; less calcium is lost in urine.

ci.why: Ineffective when eGFR is very low
x: Causes severe hyperkalaemia
Thiazides lower K⁺; at a low eGFR they just don't work.
Converts to a nephrotoxic metabolite
No toxic metabolite; they're ineffective at very low eGFR.
Too powerful: causes massive diuresis
The opposite: little drug reaches its site, so they don't work.

items.name: Loop diuretics
items.how: Block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb → large natriuresis
hx: Block NKCC2 in the collecting duct → mild natriuresis
NKCC2 is in the thick ascending limb, and the natriuresis is large.
Block aldosterone-driven Na⁺ reabsorption in the loop of Henle → natriuresis
Aldosterone acts in the collecting duct; loop diuretics block NKCC2.
Hold water in the tubule osmotically → large diuresis
That's mannitol; loop diuretics block NKCC2.
items.sewhy: Blocking NKCC2 loses sodium, potassium, magnesium and water in large amounts (low electrolytes, dehydration, AKI); they compete with urate for excretion (gout) and affect the same transporter in the inner ear (ototoxicity at high IV doses).

ci.why: Further fluid loss → shock and AKI
x: Fluid shifts into cells → cerebral oedema
The danger is further fluid loss: shock and AKI.
BP rises dangerously as the kidneys compensate
BP falls further; fluid loss causes shock and AKI.
Causes hyperkalaemia in a dry patient
Loops lower K⁺; the risk is further volume loss.
Will overcorrect the deficit
They waste Na⁺ and K⁺, making it worse.
Hides the deficit on blood tests
No masking; they deepen the deficit.
Won't work until it's corrected
They still work, causing further losses.
Precipitates in the tubules and blocks them
No crystals; they need tubular flow to reach their target.
Raises potassium in anuric patients
Loops lower K⁺; without urine flow they simply can't act.
Toxic metabolites build up and cause seizures
Not the reason; with no urine flow they can't reach NKCC2.
Additive hepatotoxicity
Neither is notably hepatotoxic; both can damage hearing.
Furosemide inactivates gentamicin in the blood
No inactivation; both are ototoxic.
Additive hyperkalaemia
Loops lower K⁺; the concern is hearing.

items.name: Mineralocorticoid antagonists
items.how: Block aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
hx: Block aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal cortex
They block the receptor; aldosterone is still made.
Block ENaC channels in the collecting duct
ENaC block is amiloride; these block the aldosterone receptor.
Block aldosterone receptors in the thick ascending limb
The receptors that matter are in the collecting duct.
items.sewhy: Blocking aldosterone means the kidney keeps potassium and loses sodium; spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors (gynaecomastia), which eplerenone mostly avoids.

ci.why: Blocks the main route for K⁺ excretion
x: Shifts K⁺ out of cells
No shift; blocking aldosterone stops renal K⁺ excretion.
Increases K⁺ absorption from the gut
No gut effect; it stops K⁺ being excreted.
Causes rhabdomyolysis, releasing K⁺
Not the mechanism; it blocks renal K⁺ excretion.
Can't excrete the drug → gynaecomastia
Gynaecomastia is a side effect, but the danger in CKD is hyperkalaemia.
Directly nephrotoxic, speeding up CKD
Not nephrotoxic; with a low GFR, K⁺ can't be excreted.
Can't excrete Na⁺ → fluid overload
They increase Na⁺ excretion; K⁺ retention is the danger.
Already cortisol-excess
Addison's is a deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone.
Already hypokalaemic
Addison's causes high K⁺ because there's no aldosterone.
Already sodium-overloaded
Addison's loses Na⁺; there's no aldosterone left to block.

items.name: Nitrates
items.how: Release NO → ↑ cGMP → venodilation (↓ preload) ± coronary dilation
hx: Release NO → ↓ cGMP → arteriolar constriction (↑ afterload)
NO raises cGMP, relaxing mainly veins (↓ preload).
Release NO → ↑ cAMP → arteriolar dilation (↓ afterload) only
NO works through cGMP, and nitrates mainly dilate veins.
Release adenosine → coronary dilation (↑ O₂ supply)
They donate NO; the main benefit is venodilation lowering preload.
items.sewhy: Nitrates release NO, which dilates veins and meningeal arteries: postural hypotension, dizziness, flushing and headache. Continuous exposure depletes the pathway, causing tolerance, so a nitrate-free period is needed.

x: Both lower cGMP → coronary spasm
Both raise cGMP; together they drop BP profoundly.
Sildenafil blocks nitrate metabolism → headache
No metabolic interaction; additive cGMP causes hypotension.
Both raise heart rate → angina
The danger is profound hypotension.
Rebound hypertension
They lower BP further.
Methaemoglobinaemia
Rare at normal doses; the risk is a further BP drop.
Fluid overload
No; venodilation drops BP further.

ci.why: Preload drop with fixed outflow → collapse
x: Afterload rise with fixed outflow → LV failure
Nitrates lower preload; with a fixed outflow, output falls.
Faster valve calcification → worse stenosis
No effect on calcification; preload drops.
Bradycardia slows filling → collapse
The problem is less preload against a fixed outflow.
RV output depends on afterload
The RV needs preload, which nitrates remove.
Nitrates constrict the right coronary artery
They dilate coronaries; the issue is the RV's preload dependence.
RV infarcts cause hypertension
They tend to cause hypotension; nitrates worsen it.

items.name: Ivabradine

uses.t: HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR ≥75

items.how: Blocks the funny current (If) in the SA node → ↓ heart rate only
hx: Blocks the funny current (If) in the AV node → ↓ AV conduction only
If is the SA node's pacemaker current; ivabradine slows the sinus rate only.
Opens K⁺ channels in the SA node → ↓ heart rate only
It blocks the If (HCN) current, not K⁺ channels.
Activates muscarinic receptors in the SA node → ↓ heart rate only
No muscarinic action; it blocks the If current.
items.sewhy: Ivabradine blocks HCN channels in the SA node (slowing the heart) and similar channels in the retina, causing transient bright flashes (phosphenes).

ci.why: Acts only on the SA node, so it doesn't work
x: Speeds the ventricular rate in AF
It neither speeds nor slows AF; it only acts on the SA node.
Converts AF to atrial flutter
No; it just doesn't work without sinus rhythm.
Raises the stroke risk in AF
Not through clotting; it only acts on the SA node.
Causes rebound tachycardia
It slows the rate further.
Blocks AV conduction completely
It acts on the SA node, so the rate slows further.
Lowers BP through vasodilation
No vasodilation; it slows the sinus rate.
Contractility may be compensating
Ivabradine doesn't affect contractility; slowing a compensating heart rate is the risk.
It extends the infarct by vasoconstriction
No vasoconstriction; slowing a compensating rate can drop output.
It's ineffective after an MI
It would work; slowing the rate is the danger.

items.name: Digoxin

uses.t: AF rate control (sedentary or with HF)

items.how: Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑ contractility; ↑ vagal tone slows AV conduction
hx: Stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑ contractility; ↓ vagal tone slows AV conduction
It inhibits the pump (raising cell Ca²⁺) and increases vagal tone.
Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 → ↑ cAMP and contractility; speeds AV conduction
That's milrinone-type action; digoxin slows the AV node.
Opens L-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↑ contractility and SA node rate
Ca²⁺ rises indirectly (through the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger), and the heart rate slows.
items.sewhy: Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and increases vagal tone; in excess this affects the gut (nausea), retina (yellow-green vision), brain (confusion) and makes cardiac cells excitable, causing almost any arrhythmia, worse with hypokalaemia.

x: Speeds AV conduction → VT
Digoxin slows AV conduction, worsening the block.
Lowers contractility, worsening output
Digoxin increases contractility; it further slows the AV node.
Causes coronary vasospasm
Not the reason; it slows the AV node further.

ci.why: Blocking the AV node pushes conduction down the accessory pathway → VF
x: Speeding the AV node lets every atrial impulse through → VF
Digoxin slows the AV node; that diverts impulses down the accessory pathway.
Blocking the accessory pathway forces conduction through the AV node → heart block
It doesn't block the pathway; it can speed conduction down it.
Raising vagal tone slows the accessory pathway → asystole
The pathway isn't slowed; AF impulses rush down it.

ci.why: Low K⁺ increases digoxin binding → toxicity
x: Low K⁺ reduces digoxin binding, so it stops working
Digoxin and K⁺ compete for the pump; low K⁺ means more digoxin binds.
Low K⁺ speeds digoxin's renal clearance → under-dosing
No; low K⁺ increases binding and toxicity.
Digoxin lowers K⁺ further → paralysis
Toxicity raises K⁺ if anything; low K⁺ makes digoxin more toxic.
Hepatically cleared → accumulates
Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys, so it builds up in CKD.
Nephrotoxic → worsens CKD
Not nephrotoxic; it accumulates because it's renally cleared.
Loses its effect as GFR falls
It becomes more potent (accumulates), not less.

items.name: Amiodarone

uses.t: VF/pulseless VT arrest (300 mg after 3rd shock)

items.how: Class III antiarrhythmic: prolongs repolarisation (K⁺ channel block); also β-, Ca²⁺- and Na⁺-blocking effects
hx: Class I antiarrhythmic: blocks Na⁺ channels to slow conduction; no other actions
Amiodarone is class III (K⁺ block) with actions of all four classes.
Class II antiarrhythmic: β-blockade only, slowing the AV node
β-block is one effect, but its main action is K⁺ channel block (class III).
Class III antiarrhythmic: shortens repolarisation (K⁺ channel opening); also α-blocking effects
It prolongs repolarisation by blocking K⁺ channels.
items.sewhy: Amiodarone is iodine-rich (thyroid dysfunction), highly fat-soluble with a very long half-life, so it accumulates in lungs, liver, skin and cornea, causing fibrosis, hepatitis, grey skin and deposits; it also prolongs repolarisation (long QT).

ci.c: Sinus bradycardia or heart block (not paced)
x: Speeds conduction → VT
Amiodarone slows conduction further.
Raises K⁺, which blocks conduction
No K⁺ effect; it directly depresses the SA and AV nodes.
Causes acute pulmonary fibrosis
Fibrosis is a long-term side effect, not the reason here.
Iodine-deficient: triggers goitre and hypothyroidism
Amiodarone is iodine-rich and can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism.
Blocks TSH release: triggers central hypothyroidism
Not through TSH; its iodine load and direct effects disturb the thyroid.
Binds thyroxine in the gut: stops levothyroxine working
That's calcium and iron; amiodarone's iodine content disrupts the thyroid.
Complete heart block
QT prolongation leads to torsades.
Atrial flutter
Torsades (polymorphic VT) is the QT risk.
Supraventricular tachycardia
Torsades is the danger.
Enzyme induction lowers their levels
Amiodarone inhibits enzymes (and P-gp), raising levels.
Protein-binding displacement lowers their levels
The main effect is raised levels from enzyme inhibition.
Reduced absorption makes them ineffective
Levels rise, risking bleeding, digoxin toxicity and myopathy.

items.name: Statins
items.how: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↑ hepatic LDL receptors → ↓ LDL
hx: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ hepatic LDL receptors → ↑ HDL only
Less liver cholesterol raises LDL receptors, which clear LDL from the blood.
Block cholesterol absorption in the gut → ↓ LDL
That's ezetimibe; statins block cholesterol synthesis in the liver.
Inhibit lipoprotein lipase → ↓ triglycerides and LDL
Lipoprotein lipase breaks down triglycerides; statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.
items.sewhy: Statins reduce cholesterol synthesis in muscle as well as liver, depleting molecules like coenzyme Q10 and causing myalgia and, rarely, rhabdomyolysis (more with CYP3A4 inhibitors). Liver enzymes may rise slightly.

ci.why: Cholesterol is needed for fetal development; stop 3 months before conception
x: They cause gestational diabetes; stop at conception
The concern is fetal development; stop 3 months before trying to conceive.
They cause a rebound rise in maternal LDL; stop after the first trimester
Stop before conception: the fetus needs cholesterol synthesis.
They pass into milk and cause neonatal myopathy; stop at delivery
They're avoided in both; the reason is the fetus's need for cholesterol.
Nephrotoxic
The concern is the liver.
Causes hypoglycaemia
No; statins can raise transaminases (hepatotoxic).
Raises ammonia
Not the reason; they're hepatotoxic.
CYP3A4 induction → statin loss → raised cholesterol
Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels.
Protein-binding displacement → liver failure
It's CYP3A4 inhibition causing statin build-up and myopathy.
Statins block clarithromycin absorption → treatment failure
No absorption effect; the statin builds up.

items.name: Alpha-blockers
items.how: Block α1 receptors → arteriolar dilation and prostate smooth-muscle relaxation
hx: Block α2 receptors → ↓ noradrenaline release and prostate shrinkage
They block α1; prostate shrinkage is what 5α-reductase inhibitors do.
Stimulate α1 receptors → arteriolar constriction and bladder neck closure
They block α1, relaxing arterioles and prostate smooth muscle.
Block β2 receptors → venous dilation and bladder relaxation
The target is the α1 receptor.
items.sewhy: Blocking α1 receptors relaxes vascular smooth muscle, so blood pressure falls on standing (especially after the first dose), causing dizziness.

ci.c: History of postural hypotension or micturition syncope
ci.why: Worsens the BP drop on standing
x: Causes urinary retention on standing
They relieve retention; the issue is the postural BP drop.
Slows the heart on standing
They don't slow the heart; BP drops on standing.
Raises BP on standing
They lower BP, worsening postural drops.
